notes.meaning: The Messiah calls out to distant Gentile lands and island nations to pay close attention to His voice. He announces that the Lord appointed Him and gave Him His saving name before He was even born.

God gave His Servant words as sharp as a sword to pierce human hearts and defeat evil. The Lord kept Him hidden and protected under His hand, like a polished arrow resting safely in a quiver until the right moment.

The Lord addresses His Servant as Israel because He stands as the true representative of God's chosen people. Through this faithful Servant, the Lord will put His own glory on display before the world.

differ.view: Calvin taught that the name Israel here includes the whole Christian church alongside Christ, rather than pointing to Jesus alone.
Guzik teaches that the Servant is Jesus alone, who represents the nation and perfectly lives out the meaning of Israel.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some older scholars argued that the servant was the entire Jewish nation, while others questioned whether the name Israel belonged in the original text.

notes.meaning: The Servant laments that His hard work seemed fruitless because so few of His own people listened to Him. Even so, He does not despair, choosing to leave His vindication and final reward in God's hands.

The Lord shaped the Servant from birth for the special task of bringing Jacob's family back to God. Even if the nation refuses to return, the Servant remains honored by the Lord, who gives Him all the strength He needs.

differ.view: MacArthur teaches that ethnic Israel will complete its worldwide missionary task in the future tribulation through 144,000 Jewish witnesses.
Guzik holds that this verse points to a future day when ethnic Israel will turn back to God and be saved.

notes.meaning: The Lord tells the Servant that restoring the small surviving remnant of Israel is too small a mission for Him. God therefore appoints Him to be a shining light to the non-Jewish nations, carrying salvation to the farthest ends of the earth.

The Lord speaks to His Servant who was mocked by ordinary people, hated by the nation, and treated like a slave of rulers. A day is coming when earthly kings and princes will stand up in deep respect and bow down before Him because the faithful God chose Him.

God promises to hear and support His Servant at the exact right moment of mercy and deliverance. The Lord gives Him to be the living guarantee of the covenant, restoring the ruined land and handing back forgotten family properties.

differ.view: Calvin emphasized that the day of salvation highlights God's free grace alone, showing that this special gift is not offered every day.
Adam Clarke viewed the day of salvation as announcing the whole gospel age, when God freely gives saving grace to all through Christ.
Ellicott explained that while the words first pictured a physical return to the land, Christians should see them fulfilled as a spiritual inheritance.

notes.meaning: The Servant commands captives to walk out of prison and tells those trapped in the dark to step into the open light. God's released people will travel like a well-fed flock, finding plenty of food even along dry, barren hills.

The returning travelers will never suffer from empty stomachs, thirst, or blistering desert heat. The God of deep mercy will shepherd them gently and guide their steps straight to cool bubbling springs of water.
The Lord promises to level rugged mountains and raise up smooth highways across the desert. He removes every hard barrier so His travelers have a clear, safe journey back home.
God's scattered family will travel from distant locations to reunite. They will stream in from the north, from the west, and from far-off southern regions.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern writers believe the gathering from distant lands is being fulfilled today as Jewish people move back to the land of Israel.

notes.meaning: The sky, the land, and the mountains are called to break out into cheerful singing. The Lord has brought comfort to His grieving people and shown tender love to those who suffered.
During their long captivity, the people of Jerusalem felt completely abandoned and forgotten by God. Their painful circumstances tempted them to doubt whether the Lord still cared for them at all.

The Lord asks if a nursing mother could ever stop caring for the helpless baby she carried. Even if a human mother could fail in her affection, God's love is far greater and He will never forget His people.

The Lord has carved the image of His people right onto the palms of His hands so they are always in His sight. Even while the city's walls lie in ruins on earth, they remain constantly before His caring eyes.
Builders rush back with great speed to restore the city's fallen structures. At the same time, the cruel enemies who wrecked the land are driven out for good.

The city is invited to look all around and see her children returning together from every side. The Lord promises on His very life that she will wear these crowds with joy, just like a bride proudly wearing her wedding jewelry.
Places that once lay empty and broken will soon be crowded with so many citizens that the land will hardly hold them. Meanwhile, the conquerors who once trampled the country will be sent far away.
The children born during the dark years of exile and loss will soon complain about the lack of space. They will call out to each other to make room so everyone has a place to settle.

The city will wonder in amazement where this massive family came from after she spent years feeling childless, lonely, and cast aside. She will be delightfully shocked to see who cared for so many children while she thought she was all alone.

The Lord God declares that He will wave His hand to summon the nations and set up His flag as a gathering point. Foreign peoples will gently carry the children of God's city in their arms and on their shoulders.

Foreign kings will look after God's people like caring foster fathers, and queens will nurture them like loving mothers. Powerful leaders will bow low to the earth in deep respect, showing that anyone who places their trust in the Lord will never be disappointed.

differ.view: Calvin used this verse to teach that earthly rulers can be genuine Christians who use their royal authority to protect and support the church.
Chuck Smith explained that this passage promises a future era when earthly kings will show great respect to the nation of Israel.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern teachers link Gentile kings helping Israel to political events like the Balfour Declaration and modern diplomatic aid.

notes.meaning: A doubting question asks whether goods can really be stolen back from a giant warrior, or if captives can be pulled from a cruel ruler's grip. The people wondered how weak exiles could ever break free from a mighty power like Babylon.

The Lord answers that even the strongest tyrant will lose his captives and his stolen goods will be taken away. God Himself will go to war against anyone who attacks His people, and He will rescue their children.

The Lord warns that cruel oppressors will destroy themselves in bitter infighting, bringing their violent power to an end. Through this mighty rescue, all mankind will recognize that the Lord is the true Savior, Redeemer, and Strong One of Jacob.
